paragraphs: Perched on the blacksmith’s anvil, he spoke between puffs on his after-dinner pipe. The forge fire was out, and through the shop’s open door and narrow windows, daylight was slowly withdrawing westward toward the mountains. In the growing shadows, his listeners sat on the pile of broken wheels on the workbench, on a keg and a barrel, puffing their own after-dinner pipes and listening.

For a business partner I want a truthful man, but for company give me someone with imagination. To my mind, imagination is the spice of life. Nothing is as uninteresting as a fact: once you know it, that’s the end of it. When life becomes nothing but facts, it won’t be worth living. Yet in a few years the human race won’t have any imagination left. Education is driving it out. Look at the children. When I was young, the bogeyman was as real to me as Pa, and almost as frightening. But just yesterday I got a lecture merely for mentioning him to my nephew. It’s the same with ghosts. We were taught to believe in ghosts just as we believed in Adam or Noah. Nowadays nobody believes in them. It’s unscientific, and if you’re superstitious, people think you’re ignorant and laugh at you. Ghosts are products of the imagination, but if I imagine I see one, he’s as real to me as if he actually exists, isn’t he? So he does exist. That’s logic. You fellows have become scientific. You admit only what you can see and feel, and don’t rely on your imagination for anything. That being so, I admit myself that spirits no longer haunt the graveyard or play around your houses. I admit it because exactly the same situation existed in Harmony when I was there, and because of what Robert J. Dinkle told me about two years after he died, and because of what happened between him, me, and the Rev. Mr. Spiegelnail.

Harmony was a highly intellectual town. Almost the last man there with any imagination or interesting ideas—except me, of course—was Robert J. Dinkle. Yet he had an awful reputation. When he died, people generally said in private that Providence had removed the last remaining monument to ignorance and superstition. You see, he was always seeing things, but we put that down to his fondness for hard cider or his natural liking for jokes. With him gone, nobody was left to report on the spirit world. In fact, the light of reason, as the Rev. Mr. Spiegelnail called it, had spread so widely that the graveyard became a popular place for moonlight strolls. Even I often walked through it on my way home from Miss Wheedle’s. I was courting her then, and it never occurred to me to walk any faster there or look back over my shoulder. I didn’t believe in such nonsense. But even the most intellectual people have moments of doubt about things they know nothing about and don’t understand. One of those moments came to me when the wind sounded more mournful than usual in the trees, and the clouds raced overhead, casting strange shadows. My imagination got the better of my intellect. I hurried. I looked back over my shoulder. I shivered a little. Naturally I saw nothing in the graveyard, but when I reached the edge of town I was still uneasy, though half laughing at myself. It was so quiet. Not a light burned anywhere, and the square seemed lonelier than the cemetery. The store looked so deserted, so ghostly in the moonlight, that I couldn’t help peering around at it.
Then, from the empty porch, from the empty bench—empty, I swear, because the night was so clear I could see perfectly—from absolutely nothing came as pleasant a voice as I ever heard.
“Hello!” it said.
My blood turned icy, and waves of chills ran up and down through me. I couldn’t move.
The voice came again, so natural and familiar that I warmed up a little, rubbed my eyes, and stared.
There on the bench, in his favorite place, sat the late Robert J. Dinkle. He gleamed in the moonlight, and the front door showed right through him.
“I must look pretty clear,” he said proudly. “Can’t you see me very plainly?”

See him plainly! I should think so. Even the patches on his coat were visible. Apart from the building showing through him, he had never looked more natural, and hearing him speak so pleasantly set me thinking. This, I told myself, is the spirit of the late Robert J. Dinkle. In life he never did me any harm, and in his present misty state he’s likely to do even less. If he’s looking for trouble, I’m not afraid of a bit of fog. That being so, I decided, I’ll speak to him as soon as I can.
But Robert got tired of waiting. He spoke again, anxiously, a little louder, and sounding rather aggrieved. “Don’t I show up well?” he said.
“I’ve never seen you looking better,” I answered. My voice had come back, the chills had eased, and I was fairly calm. I even dared to move a little closer.

A bright smile appeared on his pale face. “It’s a relief to be seen at last,” he cried cheerfully. “For years I’ve been trying to do a little haunting around here, and nobody would notice me. I used to think perhaps my material was too delicate and gauzy, but I’ve concluded that the stuff itself isn’t to blame after all.”

He gave such a natural sigh that I forgot he was a ghost. Taking him all in all, I could see he had improved. He was more solemn, had a sweeter expression, and seemed unlikely to fall back into his old habit of joking.
“Sit down and we’ll talk it over,” he went on charmingly. “Really, I can’t do any harm. But please be a little afraid, and then I’ll show up more clearly. I must be getting dim now.”
“You are,” I said. Although I was on the porch and boldly edging nearer to him, I could hardly see him.
Without warning, he let out a terrible groan that sent the chills surging back. I jumped and stared, and as I stared, he stood out clearer and more solid in the moonlight.
“That’s better,” he said with a merry chuckle. “Now you believe in me, don’t you? Well, sit there nervously on the edge of the bench, and don’t get too calm or I’ll disappear.”

I followed the ghost’s orders exactly. But with him sitting there so naturally and pleasantly, it was hard to stay frightened, and more than once I forgot. When he saw me peering as though my eyesight was failing, he would give a bloodcurdling groan. Up he would flare again, gleaming in the moonlight, full and strong.

“Harmony’s getting too scientific, too intellectual,” he said mournfully. “Anything arithmetic or geography can’t explain is dismissed as impossible. Even the preachers encourage these ideas and talk about Adam and Eve being allegories. As a result, the graveyard has become the dullest place in town. You simply can’t haunt anything around here. A man hears a groan in his room, and he gets up and fastens the shutters more tightly, or throws a shoe at a rat, or curses the wind in the chimney. A few spirits were hanging around when I first died, but they complained bitterly about the hard times. They said there used to be plenty of good company in the graveyard, but one by one they’d had to give up. All the old Berrys had left. Mr. Whoople retired after someone mistook him for a white mule. Mrs. Morris A. Klump, who used to operate around the deserted house beyond the mill, gave up in disgust just a week before I arrived. I tried to encourage the few who remained. I explained that the spiritualists were working their way down the valley and would reach town any time. But they’d lost all hope. They kept fading away until I was the only one left. If things don’t improve soon, I’ll have to go too. It’s terribly discouraging. And lonely! People wander around the graves as though even I weren’t there. Just last night my boy Ossy came strolling along with the lady he’s courting. Where do you suppose they sat down to rest, look at the moon, and talk about the silliest things? Right on my headstone! I stood in front of them and did the ghostliest things until I was completely worn out and discouraged. They simply wouldn’t pay the slightest attention.”
The poor old ghost almost broke down and cried. I had never known him so moved in life. Seeing him wipe his eyes with his handkerchief and sniffle touched me deeply.
“Perhaps you don’t make enough noise when you haunt,” I said sympathetically.

“I do all the usual acts,” he said, a little irritated by my remark. “We’ve always been rather limited. I float around and groan, talk nonsense, and sometimes pull the covers off beds or reveal where treasure is buried. But what good does that do in a town as intellectual as Harmony?”

I’ve seen many people down on their luck, but nobody ever moved me as much as the late Robert J. Dinkle. It was his voice, his looks, his general air of misery, his helplessness, and how much he deserved help. I had known him well in life, and I liked him even better as he was now. I truly wanted to do something for him. We sat thinking for a long time. He smoked furiously, blowing clouds of fog from his pipe, while I tried to think of a way to help. And ideas always come to those who sit and wait.

“The trouble is partly what you say, Robert,” I admitted after a while, “and partly that you can’t make enough noise to wake the sleeping imagination of intellectual Harmony. But with a little natural help from me, you might stir things up in this town.”
You never saw a happier smile or a more grateful look than that poor spirit gave me.
“Ah,” he said, “with your help I could do wonders. Who shall we start with?”
“The Rev. Mr. Spiegelnail,” I said, “has about all the imagination left in Harmony—except me, of course.”
Robert’s face visibly fell. “I’ve tried him again and again,” he said, sounding rather argumentative. “His only response was to complain that his wife talked in her sleep.”

I wasn’t going to argue—not me. I was all for action, and wasted no time getting started. Robert J. followed me like a dog, up through town to our house. I went inside, leaving him outside so he wouldn’t disturb Mother. I got a hammer, some nails, and the heavy lead weight from my fishing net. Before long, I had the finest window-knocking contraption you ever saw working against the Spiegelnails’ parlor window. I hid in a lilac bush, pulling the string that kept the weight swinging. There was an open patch in front of the house where the moon shone full and clear. Robert J. walked up and down there, about two feet above the ground, slowly waving his arms and giving the most mournful groans. Now, I’ve been to see Uncle Tom’s Cabin plenty of times, but I never saw acting like that in my life. And what happened? The upstairs window went up, and the Rev. Mr. Spiegelnail appeared plainly in the moonlight.
“Who’s there?” he called sternly. You should have seen Robert then. It was like a tonic to him. He rose higher, began thrashing his arms, and gurgled mightily. But the preacher never moved.
“You boys should be ashamed of yourselves,” he said severely.
“Louder, louder,” I called to Robert J. In response, he began twisting himself into the most dreadful shapes.
“You can hear me perfectly well,” the minister said, sounding sad now. “It fills my old heart with sorrow to see you all going so far astray.”

Hearing him so calm, so clear, and so defiant made Robert J. stop short and stare. To remind him, I gave the weight an extra thump. It was so loud that it brought Mrs. Spiegelnail to the window. Her head showed clearly as she peered over the preacher’s shoulder. The poor, discouraged ghost took heart and struck his most tragic pose. He told me afterward that he had got it from a book and was especially proud of it. But what was the result?
“Do you hear someone in the bushes, dear?” Mr. Spiegelnail asked, turning his head to listen.
“It must be Ossy Dinkle and those bad friends of his,” she said sourly.
Poor Robert! Hearing that, he almost gave up hope.
“Don’t I show up well?” he asked anxiously.
“I can see you clearly,” I said sharply. “You’ve never looked better.”
Down went the window, so suddenly and unexpectedly that I didn’t know what to make of it. Robert J. thought he understood, and came floating over to me, delighted.

“I must have worked,” he said, laughing as though he would die, doubling over and holding his sides to keep them from splitting. “At last I’ve shown up clearly. At last I’m some use in the world. You don’t realize what a pleasure it is to know you’re fulfilling your mission and living up to your reputation.”

Poor old ghost! He wanted to talk it all over then and there. He settled on a soft cluster of lilacs, smoking fog and chattering away. It did me good to see him so happy, and I was feeling rather proud of my own success in the haunting business. But that didn’t last long. A rattle of keys warned us. The front door flew open, and out bounded the Rev. Mr. Spiegelnail. He cleared the steps in one jump and flew across the lawn. All thought of the late Robert J. Dinkle left me then: I had only a few feet’s head start on my pastor. You see, I wouldn’t have hurried so much, except that I sang bass in the choir. I doubted I could convince him I was working in the interests of Science and Truth. Running was instinctive. Gates didn’t matter; I sailed over them. Down the street I went with the preacher’s hot breath on my neck. But I beat him. He tired after his first burst and soon fell behind, so I could double back home to bed.
Robert wanted to give up altogether.

“I simply won’t work,” he told me when I met him on the store porch the next night. “A hundred years ago, a bit of haunting like that would have emptied the town. Today it gets put down to natural causes.”
“Because,” I said, “we left evidence of physical activity behind: strings and weights on the parlor window.”
“Suppose we work inside the house?” he suggested, brightening. “You could hide in the closet and groan while I act.”
Now, did you ever hear anything so innocent? But he meant so well that I didn’t even laugh.

“I’m too fond of my pastor,” I said, “to let him catch me in his closet. A much better place for us to work is the shortcut he takes home from church after the Wednesday evening meeting. We won’t be so loud. We’ll be more dignified, mournful, and tragic. You overacted last night, Robert,” I told him. “Next time, pace up and down as though you’re deep in thought, and sigh gently. Then, if he sees you, it would be nice to take his arm and walk home with him.”

I think I had the right idea about haunting. If I’d been able to keep Robert J. Dinkle’s spirits up and train him regularly, I could have awakened Harmony’s sleeping imagination and brought life to the graveyard. But he was too easily discouraged. He lacked perseverance. If Mr. Spiegelnail ever came close to seeing things, it was that night when he stepped out of the woods. He had been walking slowly and thoughtfully until he came opposite my hiding place. Now, I didn’t howl or groan or say anything in particular. I made a noise that wasn’t animal, wasn’t human, and wasn’t the usual ghostly sort either. As I had told the late Robert J. Dinkle, haunting needed something new and original. And it certainly caught Mr. Spiegelnail’s attention. I saw him stop. I saw his lantern shake. He looked as though he was going to dive into the bushes after me, but he changed his mind. On he went, faster, as though he wasn’t afraid and yet he was. He went on into the open, where the moon showed Robert beautifully as he paced slowly back and forth, his head bowed as though thinking hard. Still the preacher didn’t see him. In fact, he walked right through him. I made the dreadful sound again. That stopped him. He turned, raised the lantern in front of him, put a hand to his ear, and seemed to look and listen intently. Robert stood barely ten feet away, trembling with excitement. But the light shining through him remained rock steady as the minister watched and listened, so quiet and calm. He lowered the lantern, rubbed his eyes, stepped forward, and looked again. The ghost was perfect. As I said, he was excited and his sigh shook a little, but he was full of dignity and sadness. He shouldn’t have lost heart so soon. I was sure he had almost become clearly visible to the preacher. He would have grown clearer to Mr. Spiegelnail if he had kept haunting him, instead of giving up because the pastor walked home fairly calmly that one night. I know he walked faster. He looked over his shoulder twice, and I heard the kitchen door slam with relief. But when we consider what ghosts are made of, we shouldn’t expect them to be heroes. They’re too foggy and gauzy to have much perseverance—judging by Robert J., anyway.
“I simply can’t work anymore,” he said when I went up to him. He sat in the path, elbows on his knees, head in his hands, staring mournfully at the ground.
“But Robert—” I began, hoping to cheer him up.
He didn’t hear. He wouldn’t listen. He just faded away.

If he had only held on, there’s no telling what he might have achieved in his line of work. I’ve often thought about him since, and considered his tremendous possibilities. I’m certain he had possibilities. If I’d realized it on that last night we went haunting, he would never have got away from me. But I realized it too late. It came to me in church the very next Sunday, during the usual announcements after the long prayer. Mr. Spiegelnail was leaning over the pulpit, surveying the congregation through large dark-tinted glasses.

“I regret to announce,” he said sadly, “that for the first time in twenty years, the town’s churches will hold joint services next Sunday.” Sitting in the choir, reading my musical notation, I heard the preacher’s words and started. I could see at once that something unusual was happening, or had happened, or was about to happen. “Unfortunately,” Mr. Spiegelnail continued, “I shall have to hand my pulpit over to Brother Spiker of the Baptist Church. My failing eyesight makes it necessary for me to go immediately to Philadelphia to consult an eye specialist. Some of my dear brothers and sisters may think this an unusual step, but I would not abandon them without reason. Perhaps they think I’m making a great fuss over nothing and could be treated just as well in Harrisburg. To them, let me explain that I suffer from astigmatism. It isn’t so much that I can’t see, but that I see things I know aren’t there—a fault in my sight that I feel needs the most expert attention. Sunday school at nine-thirty; worship at eleven. My text is: ‘And the old men shall see visions.’”

How I wished the late Robert J. Dinkle could have been in church that morning! It would have made him so happy to hear that he had partly worked. If he worked partly, surely in time he would work completely. As for me, I was wild with excitement. I was so busy thinking about him and how glad he would be that I didn’t hear the sermon at all. Planning new ways to haunt, I forgot to sing in the last anthem. You see, I imagined lively times ahead for Harmony: a general return to the good old days when people had imagination and something besides facts in their heads. I only had to find Robert again. With him working, it wouldn’t be long before all the old Berrys and Mrs. Klump appeared clearly and plainly. But I didn’t understand how weak ghosts’ characters are. I thought, of course, that I could easily find my spirit friend when night came. Yet I couldn’t. I sat shivering on the store porch until the moon stood high above the ridge. He simply wouldn’t come. I called softly for him and got no answer. I went down to the graveyard and sat on his headstone. It was the quietest place you ever saw. Clouds raced overhead. The wind sighed in the leaves. Through the trees, the moon shone so clearly and brightly that you could almost read the monuments. It was just the kind of night when things should have been lively there—a perfect night for haunting. I called for Robert. I listened. He never answered. I heard only a bullfrog bellowing in the pond, a whippoorwill whistling in the grove, and a dog howling at the moon.
